r: RA 9522 (baselines law) is constitutional. UNCLOS III and baselines laws do not add to or reduce territory; States acquire or lose territory only by occupation, accretion, cession and prescription. Treating the Kalayaan Island Group and Scarborough Shoal as a ‘regime of islands’ does not cede them.
f: Law professors and students, as citizens and taxpayers, challenged the 2009 baselines law for allegedly shrinking territory and converting internal waters into archipelagic waters.
h: Petition dismissed; RA 9522 upheld.
x: West Philippine Sea stories: distinguish territory (sovereignty) from maritime zones (sovereign rights under UNCLOS). Also applies to the Maritime Zones Act (RA 12064, 2024) and the Archipelagic Sea Lanes Act (RA 12065, 2024).

n: The South China Sea Arbitration (Philippines v. China)
r: China’s claim to historic rights within the nine-dash line has no legal basis to the extent it exceeds UNCLOS entitlements. No Spratly feature is a fully entitled island that generates an EEZ. China violated the Philippines’ sovereign rights in its EEZ.
f: The Philippines brought an UNCLOS Annex VII arbitration over China’s nine-dash line, the status of features, and Chinese conduct (fishing, reclamation, obstruction).
h: Award in favor of the Philippines on most claims (July 12, 2016). The tribunal did not rule on sovereignty over features.
x: Use for any West Philippine Sea fact pattern: maritime entitlements, EEZ rights, enforcement. Remember the award decides entitlements, not sovereignty.

n: Province of North Cotabato v. GRP Peace Panel on Ancestral Domain
r: The MOA-AD was unconstitutional: the Executive cannot guarantee constitutional amendments or create a ‘Bangsamoro Juridical Entity’ with associative status, which presupposes a State. The case was decided despite mootness (the MOA-AD was not signed) because of grave constitutional issues.
f: The GRP panel initialed a Memorandum of Agreement on Ancestral Domain with the MILF, promising to effect the constitutional and legal changes needed; a TRO stopped the signing.
h: MOA-AD declared contrary to law and the Constitution.
x: Peace agreement stories: the President may negotiate and propose but cannot bind Congress or the people to amend the Constitution. Contrast PHILCONSA (2016) on ripeness.

n: Cruz v. Secretary of Environment and Natural Resources
r: The constitutionality of IPRA (RA 8371) was challenged under the Regalian Doctrine. The Court was split 7–7; after redeliberation the tie remained, so the petition was dismissed and the law stands (Rule 56 on ties).
f: Citizens and taxpayers attacked IPRA’s recognition of ancestral domains, including natural resources, as ‘private but community property’ of indigenous peoples.
h: Petition dismissed on a tie vote; IPRA not declared unconstitutional.
x: Use for the effect of a tie vote and for native title versus the Regalian Doctrine (Puno’s separate opinion). Also listed under Judiciary (Voting).

r: A natural-born Filipino who reacquires citizenship under RA 9225 and runs for office must (1) take the oath of allegiance and (2) execute a personal, sworn renunciation of foreign citizenship before filing the COC. Winning the election does not cure ineligibility.
f: A naturalized US citizen reacquired Philippine citizenship, ran for Manila councilor, and won, but never executed a sworn renunciation.
h: Disqualified; COMELEC’s annulment of her proclamation was affirmed and the next-ranked qualified candidate proclaimed.
x: Dual citizen candidates. Note: the remedy of proclaiming the next-ranked candidate (the second-placer rule) was abandoned in Mangudadatu v. COMELEC (2025).

r: An illegitimate child of a Filipino father and an alien mother is a Filipino citizen if paternity is proven; the 1935 Constitution’s ‘father is a citizen’ rule draws no distinction by legitimacy. Evidence suggested FPJ’s grandfather became a Filipino under the Philippine Bill of 1902.
f: Petitions to disqualify Fernando Poe Jr. for President argued he was illegitimate and so followed his American mother’s citizenship.
h: Petitions dismissed; COMELEC did not commit grave abuse in refusing to cancel the COC. Jurisdiction over a President’s qualifications after the election belongs to the PET.
x: Use for natural-born status by blood (jus sanguinis), the 1935 rules, and forum (COMELEC before the election; PET after).

r: Foundlings are natural-born citizens: the Constitution, its deliberations, the statistical probability that a child found in the Philippines has Filipino parents, and international law support a presumption of Filipino parentage. Grace Poe was qualified as Senator.
f: A defeated senatorial candidate filed quo warranto in the SET, arguing Senator Poe, a foundling, was not natural-born.
h: The SET did not commit grave abuse; petition dismissed.
x: Foundling status and the SET’s jurisdiction over a sitting Senator’s qualifications.
g: Gatmaytan, ‘Hard Cases Make Bad Movies: The Candidates Poe and Philippine Citizenship Law as Screenplay’ (2021) is assigned with this case. The Poe cases appeared on his 2015 midterm (forum, ripeness, and whether the SET and the PET may reach different results).

r: Election of Philippine citizenship (for those born of Filipino mothers before Jan. 17, 1973) may be implied from positive acts such as voting and holding office. A person whose father was naturalized while he was a minor, and who elected, is natural-born. Residence means domicile and is not lost by temporary absence.
f: Jose Ong Jr., born in Samar to a Chinese father later naturalized and a Filipina mother, was elected to Congress; losing candidates said he was not natural-born or a resident.
h: HRET ruling upheld; Ong was natural-born and a resident. The Court reviews the HRET only for grave abuse.
x: Election of citizenship; who is natural-born under Art. IV, Sec. 2; and HRET deference.

r: A naturalized Filipino who later obtains and uses a foreign passport and declares a foreign nationality in documents expressly renounces Philippine citizenship. Citizenship is not a commodity to be displayed when required and suppressed when convenient.
f: A naturalized Filipino of Portuguese origin renewed and used a Portuguese passport and described himself as Portuguese in business papers.
h: He was held to have lost Philippine citizenship; his detention for deportation was valid.
x: Loss of citizenship by express renunciation through conduct.

r: Repatriation under RA 8171 is done by filing with the Special Committee on Naturalization, not the regional trial court. An RTC that grants repatriation acts without jurisdiction.
f: A natural-born Filipino who became a US citizen petitioned the RTC to regain citizenship and took his oath there.
h: RTC proceedings void for lack of jurisdiction.
x: Right forum and mode for reacquiring citizenship.

r: Repatriation restores a person to his original status: a natural-born Filipino who lost citizenship (here by serving in the US armed forces) and is repatriated is again natural-born and may sit in the House.
f: Teodoro Cruz, a natural-born Filipino, became a US citizen through military service, was repatriated under RA 2630, and was elected Representative.
h: Cruz was natural-born and qualified; HRET upheld.
x: Use when a former Filipino who reacquired citizenship runs for an office requiring natural-born status (compare RA 9225 reacquisition, which also restores natural-born status).

n: Tan Co v. Civil Register of Manila
r: CA 473 (minor children of a naturalized father become citizens) and the law under which the father was naturalized (LOI 270) are in pari materia: minor children of those naturalized under LOI 270 also become Filipinos.
f: Siblings sought to correct their birth records to show Philippine citizenship after their father was naturalized under LOI 270 while they were minors.
h: Correction allowed; they are Filipino citizens.
x: Derivative naturalization of minor children.

r: Election under CA 625 requires a sworn statement of election, an oath of allegiance, and registration with the civil registry, within a reasonable time (generally three years) after majority. Election cannot be done by judicial declaration.
f: A legitimate child of a Chinese father and Filipina mother took an oath 12 years after majority and never registered it, then sought a court declaration.
h: Petition dismissed; no valid election, and courts cannot declare citizenship in a petition of this kind.
x: Contrast Co v. HRET: implied election applies only to those already treated as Filipino; Sagun’s formal election was late and defective.

r: Naturalization is a privilege, strictly construed. Character witnesses must be credible persons with personal knowledge vouching for the applicant; omissions in required petition contents (e.g., former residences) are fatal.
f: A Manila-born son of Chinese parents applied for judicial naturalization under CA 473.
h: Petition denied.
x: Judicial naturalization requirements.

r: Failure to attach a certificate of arrival to a petition for naturalization is fatal; it is separate from the declaration of intention and is not excused by exemption from the latter.
f: An applicant exempt from filing a declaration of intention did not attach his certificate of arrival.
h: Petition denied.
x: Strict compliance in naturalization.

r: A ‘lucrative trade, profession or lawful occupation’ means income with an appreciable margin over expenses, proven by documents; a comfortable lifestyle is not proof.
f: An Indian national applied for naturalization but did not show his actual financial status.
h: Petition denied.
x: Strict proof of naturalization qualifications.

r: Using a foreign passport after renouncing foreign citizenship recants the renunciation; the candidate becomes a dual citizen again and is disqualified (LGC Sec. 40(d)). Where the COC is void from the start, votes for the ineligible candidate are stray.
f: Rommel Arnado reacquired citizenship and renounced US citizenship, then twice used his US passport, and won as mayor.
h: Arnado disqualified; the next-ranked qualified candidate (Maquiling) was ordered proclaimed.
x: Dual citizen candidate who keeps acting as a foreigner. Remedy update: the second-placer rule was abandoned in Mangudadatu (2025); the vacancy is now filled by succession.

r: Citizenship for a local elective official is required at the latest at proclamation or the start of the term. Repatriation under PD 725 is curative and retroacts to the date of application. A second-placer cannot be proclaimed when the winner is disqualified (except when voters knowingly threw away their votes).
f: Frivaldo, a naturalized US citizen, won as Sorsogon governor; his repatriation oath was taken on the day his term began.
h: Frivaldo was qualified; the second-placer (Lee) was not entitled to the seat.
x: Timing of the citizenship qualification for local officials; retroactive repatriation.
w: The masterfile digest’s top ‘Doctrine’ line states the opposite (that the second-placer must be declared winner). Its own Holdings section says Frivaldo won and the second-placer cannot be proclaimed. Rely on the Holdings.

r: RA 9225 requires a personal and sworn renunciation before an officer authorized to administer oaths; an unsworn renunciation filed abroad does not comply. Foreign law must be proved; it is not judicially noticed.
f: A repatriated former Australian citizen renounced Australian citizenship by an unsworn declaration and won as vice-mayor.
h: Disqualified.
x: Strict form of the renunciation; proof of foreign law.

r: RA 9225 does not violate Art. IV, Sec. 5. Dual citizenship is not dual allegiance; the law concerns only Philippine citizenship and leaves foreign citizenship to foreign law. What dual allegiance is, and how to deal with it, is for Congress to define.
f: A petition for prohibition argued that letting reacquiring Filipinos keep foreign citizenship sanctions dual allegiance.
h: RA 9225 upheld.
x: Use against claims that dual citizens are ‘unconstitutional’ or that a body like the CSC may bar them without a law.
g: Gatmaytan’s book quotes the point that the Court cannot set the parameters of dual allegiance because the Constitution left that to Congress.

r: The RA 9225 oath-and-renunciation requirements apply only to dual citizens by naturalization who reacquire Philippine citizenship. A dual citizen by birth (Filipino father, American mother) need not renounce; filing a COC is itself an implied renunciation.
f: A Makati-born candidate for councilor with a Filipino father and American mother was disqualified by COMELEC for not renouncing US citizenship (based on a Consular Report of Birth Abroad).
h: COMELEC reversed; she was qualified. The consular report only recognized, not conferred, US citizenship.
x: Distinguish dual citizens by birth (no RA 9225 steps; Mercado v. Manzano rule) from those who reacquired citizenship (two-step RA 9225).

r: For election purposes, residence means domicile. Domicile is not lost by working and even voting elsewhere unless three things concur: physical presence in the new place, intention to remain there, and intention to abandon the old domicile.
f: A man from Abuyog worked in Bukidnon for a time (and voted there) while keeping property and family ties in Abuyog, then won as mayor of Abuyog.
h: He had not lost his Abuyog domicile; he was qualified.
x: Residence or domicile questions for voters and candidates.
test: New domicile by choice: (1) bodily presence in the new place; (2) animus manendi (intent to remain); (3) animus non revertendi (intent to abandon the old).

r: A change of domicile must be voluntary. Leaving the country out of fear for one’s safety after EDSA is not abandonment of domicile.
f: Philip Romualdez fled to the US in 1986, returned in 1991, and registered in his old barangay in Leyte; his exclusion from the voters’ list was sought.
h: He remained a resident and a qualified voter.
x: Involuntary absence does not change domicile.

r: Registration is a valid procedural regulation of suffrage, not a substantive requirement. COMELEC cannot be compelled to hold special registration within the 120-day prohibitive period of RA 8189, Sec. 8, and its ‘stand-by’ power may be used only if pre-election acts cannot reasonably be held within the law’s periods.
f: Youth groups sought a two-day special registration in February 2001, within 120 days of the May 2001 election.
h: Petitions dismissed.
x: Registration deadlines that fall within the statutory prohibitive period. Contrast Palatino.

r: Biometrics validation (RA 10367) is part of registration, a procedural regulation, not a ‘qualification’ or a prohibited ‘substantive requirement’ under Art. V, Sec. 1. It also passes strict scrutiny: a compelling interest in a clean voters’ list, pursued by the least restrictive means (deactivated voters may reactivate).
f: ‘No Bio, No Boto’: COMELEC would deactivate about 2.4 to 3 million voters without biometrics before the 2016 elections.
h: RA 10367 and the COMELEC resolutions upheld; the earlier TRO was lifted.
x: The 2015 Finals asked exactly this. Any new condition on voting: is it a qualification (only the Constitution and laws within Art. V may impose) or a registration procedure (valid if reasonable)?

r: COMELEC cannot cut short the continuing registration Congress fixed in RA 8189, Sec. 8 (registration closes only 120 days before a regular election). Its stand-by power to fix other dates applies only when pre-election acts cannot reasonably be held within the statutory period, which COMELEC must show.
f: For the 2010 elections, COMELEC moved the registration deadline to October 31, 2009, months before the 120-day prohibitive period.
h: Petition granted; the resolution setting the October 31 deadline was declared void and registration extended until January 9, 2010.
x: Distinguish AKBAYAN: there the extension sought fell inside the prohibitive period; here it did not. The 2015 Finals (Ridon, October 31, 2015 deadline) is a near-copy; read the dates carefully.
g: Sources differ in summaries; this card follows the masterfile digest and the 2025 Reviewer, both of which state the petition was granted.

r: Excluding voters of highly urbanized cities (and of component cities whose charters so provide) from voting for provincial officials does not violate equal protection or impose a ‘substantive requirement’: the classification by income is reasonable, and there is no right to vote for officials of a unit that does not govern you.
f: Voters of Cebu City and Mandaue City challenged BP 51, which barred them from voting for Cebu provincial officials.
h: BP 51 upheld.
x: Use when a law changes which voters may vote for which offices (e.g., new provinces, HUC conversions).

r: Absentee voting by Filipinos abroad (RA 9189) is an exception to the residence requirement under Art. V, Sec. 2; the affidavit of intent to return is valid. But a Joint Congressional Oversight Committee that reviews and approves COMELEC’s rules violates COMELEC’s independence, and COMELEC cannot canvass and proclaim the President and Vice President (Congress does).
f: A lawyer challenged several provisions of the Overseas Absentee Voting Act of 2003.
h: Law upheld except the JCOC approval provisions and the COMELEC proclamation of President and Vice President.
x: Use with ABAKADA for legislative vetoes over independent bodies; also overseas voting questions.

r: ‘Government’ in the sedition law means the system or institutions of government, not the persons who run it (the administration). Attacking officials’ character is not an attack on the government.
f: Editors were convicted of seditious libel for an editorial attacking the Civil Commission’s appointments of Filipinos.
h: Conviction reversed.
x: Distinguish ‘government’ from ‘administration’; useful when officials treat criticism as an attack on the State.

r: The National Centennial Commission chair holds a public office: the commission was created by law (executive issuance), exercised a sovereign function (promoting national culture and heritage), and served the public. The Ombudsman may investigate him even if he received no compensation.
f: Salvador Laurel, NCC chair and CEO of Expocorp, was investigated for graft over Centennial Expo contracts.
h: Petition dismissed; the Ombudsman had jurisdiction.
x: What is a public office (Mechem’s elements); ‘governmental’ functions include promotion of culture.
test: Public office (Mechem, as applied in Laurel): (1) created by law; (2) delegated a portion of sovereign power; (3) has continuance, even if temporary; (4) powers and scope defined by law; (5) exercised for the public benefit.

n: Co Kim Cham v. Valdez Tan Keh
sub: IV.C De facto and de jure government
r: The Japanese-sponsored governments were de facto governments of paramount force; their judicial acts not of a political complexion remain valid after liberation (postliminy), and restored courts may continue pending cases without an enabling law.
f: A judge refused to continue a civil case begun during the Japanese occupation, citing MacArthur’s proclamation voiding the occupation government’s processes.
h: Mandamus granted; proceedings continue.
x: Kinds of de facto government (usurper, paramount force, secession) and the validity of their acts.

r: During the interregnum (Feb. 25, 1986 to the Freedom Constitution), there was no Constitution or Bill of Rights, but the revolutionary government remained bound by the ICCPR and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Seizures beyond the warrant were invalid.
f: A raid on the house of a general’s associate seized cash, jewelry and items not listed in the warrant, under a revolutionary government.
h: Items not in the warrant were ordered returned; the PCGG also lacked jurisdiction over persons not shown to be Marcos associates.
x: Use for ‘revolutionary government’ talk in the news: a sitting president elected under the Constitution cannot declare one without repudiating that Constitution.
g: Gatmaytan’s book quotes this case for Aquino’s government being ‘indisputably revolutionary’.

r: Parens patriae lets the State protect minors but supplements, not supplants, parents’ primary right. Curfew ordinances restricting minors’ fundamental rights are tested by strict scrutiny: compelling interest plus least restrictive means.
f: Manila, Navotas and Quezon City adopted curfews for minors after Oplan Rody.
h: Manila and Navotas ordinances struck down (not narrowly drawn, penal provisions conflict with the Juvenile Justice Act); Quezon City ordinance upheld.
x: Any LGU regulation targeting minors or a vulnerable class; also a model of strict-scrutiny analysis.

r: A suit against an official is not a suit against the State if it seeks only to nullify an ultra vires act (no financial charge on the State), or if the official is sued personally for tortious acts beyond authority.
f: A DOTC undersecretary offered for bidding an orbital slot already promised to PASI under an MOU, and allegedly defamed PASI’s CEO.
h: Immunity did not bar the injunction, nullity, and damages claims against the official.
x: Whenever an official raises state immunity, ask what relief is sought and whether it would charge the treasury.
test: Suit against an officer is a suit against the State if a judgment would require the State to act or pay. Exceptions: (1) the officer acted beyond authority or illegally; (2) the State has no interest in the outcome; (3) personal liability for tort.

r: A foreign agent acting within his official functions, with the host State’s consent to his activities, shares his State’s immunity (par in parem non habet imperium). Diplomatic immunity depends on performing diplomatic functions; a DEA attaché is not automatically a diplomat.
f: An Iranian national acquitted of drug charges sued a US DEA agent who had set up a buy-bust with Philippine narcotics officers.
h: Complaint dismissed: the agent was immune as an agent of the US acting with the Philippine government’s imprimatur.
x: Foreign officials sued in Philippine courts.

r: An implementing agency of a foreign State must first be classified: if incorporated, its suability depends on its charter or the general law (‘sue and be sued’), regardless of its functions. Immunity must be properly established, e.g., by a DFA certification.
f: Filipino employees of GTZ, the German implementing agency in a health insurance project, sued for illegal dismissal; GTZ claimed immunity.
h: GTZ failed to establish immunity: it did not show it was unincorporated or immune under its own law, and had no DFA certification of immunity. Its petition was denied.
x: Foreign state enterprises and incorporated agencies.

r: The State cannot invoke immunity to avoid paying for a public work it has accepted and used; justice demands payment on quantum meruit even if the contract is void for lack of formalities.
f: A contractor completed DPWH dike works in Pampanga; DPWH refused payment, invoking immunity and a void contract.
h: Payment on quantum meruit ordered (through COA).
x: Immunity cannot be an instrument of injustice; implied consent when the State benefits.

r: US Navy officers sued for the USS Guardian’s grounding on Tubbataha Reef are immune: a suit against them in their official capacity is a suit against the United States, and the writ of kalikasan cannot be used to collect damages or nullify the VFA. The flag State bears international responsibility under UNCLOS.
f: Petitioners sought a writ of kalikasan against US officers and Philippine officials after a US minesweeper ran aground in Tubbataha in 2013.
h: Petition denied.
x: The 2013 midterm asked about this exact story (Colmenares). Foreign warship immunity, standing (Rules on Environmental Cases), and limits of kalikasan.

r: Government funds are not subject to garnishment or execution, even if an appropriation exists. Once liability is fixed by judgment, the claimant must file a money claim with COA, which has primary jurisdiction.
f: After DPWH failed to pay a compromise on just compensation for land taken for flood control, the RTC garnished DPWH funds.
h: Garnishment set aside; claim to be filed with COA, with legal interest.
x: Use when a court or claimant tries to seize public funds (consent to be sued is not consent to execution).

n: Rubi v. Provincial Board of Mindoro
r: Police power, ‘the law of overruling necessity’, justified confining the Mangyans to a reservation; the classification by degree of civilization was upheld, and delegating to the provincial board the choice of site was valid (discretion in execution, not in making the law).
f: Mangyans were ordered to live on a reservation under the Administrative Code; those who refused were detained.
h: Habeas corpus denied; law upheld (with a strong dissent on due process).
x: Historical police power case; read critically as a product of colonial policy.

r: Requiring early warning devices on motor vehicles is a valid exercise of police power; it is reasonable and not confiscatory, and the delegation to the LTO to implement it had a sufficient standard.
f: A car owner challenged LOI 229 requiring early warning triangles as oppressive and an undue delegation.
h: LOI 229 and its rules upheld.
x: Classic police power and delegation case for safety regulations.

r: Closing Boracay for six months for rehabilitation was a valid police power measure (lawful subject: environment and health; lawful means: reasonably necessary, not unduly oppressive). The effect on travel was incidental; livelihood expectancies of informal workers must yield to the general welfare.
f: Proclamation 475 declared a state of calamity and temporarily closed Boracay; a worker and a resident challenged it.
h: Petition dismissed; Proclamation 475 valid.
x: A government closure or regulation burdening businesses and workers: apply the lawful subject and lawful means test.

n: Iloilo I Electric Cooperative v. Executive Secretary
r: Public utility franchises cannot be exclusive and are subject to amendment or repeal by Congress for the common good (Art. XII, Sec. 11). Expanding MORE Power’s franchise into cooperatives’ areas (RA 11918) is valid; contract and franchise rights yield to police power.
f: Three Iloilo electric cooperatives challenged a law extending MORE Electric and Power’s franchise into their coverage areas.
h: Petition dismissed (Zalameda, J.; Leonen, J., dissenting).
x: Laws that impose new duties on regulated private businesses (franchises, utilities): non-impairment yields to police power; no exclusive franchise.
w: Do not confuse with PECO v. MORE (Iloilo City distribution assets), a different case.
